scenario: An 81-year-old male falls down stairs at home with a head injury and deteriorating level of consciousness in the setting of rivaroxaban use. The scenario focuses on recognition and management of severe traumatic brain injury, raised ICP, NOAC reversal, neuroprotective RSI, post-intubation management, and family discussion.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Sir, what brought you in today, and when did it start? Tell me how you're feeling right now.

patient_emotion.notes: [clinician: Sir, what brought you in today, and when did it start? Tell me how you're feeling right now.] The utterance is a neutral open-ended history-taking question with no bad news, no serious disclosure, no blame, and no loss content. Fear stays absent (no clinical threat disclosed). Sadness stays absent (no loss). Overwhelm stays absent (a single simple question, no informational overload). Shame stays absent (nonjudgmental, no exposure or blame).

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: I... fell. The stairs — my head, it hurts. Where... I don't— everything's spinning, I feel sick, gonna be sick. Just let me be, don't— my head...

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Let's get a 12-lead ECG on him now — he's in atrial fibrillation on the monitor.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: You fell on the stairs and hit your head. I need one thing from you right now: are you taking any blood thinners or other regular medications?

patient_emotion.notes: [clinician: You fell on the stairs and hit your head. I need one thing from you right now: are you taking any blood thinners or other regular medications?] The utterance restates a known fact (fell and hit head) and asks a focused, calm question about medications. No newly discovered serious abnormality, worsening condition, or need to escalate care is disclosed to the patient, so fear stays absent. No loss/anticipated loss language, so sadness stays absent. It is a single simple question, not an information overload, so overwhelm stays absent. No blame, judgment, or exposure, so shame stays absent.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: ECG's back — confirms atrial fibrillation. Heads up: sats are down to 91 on room air, GCS 13, and he's reporting head pain with nausea after a fall. Want me to set him up for oxygen?

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: Medications? I... I don't— pills, maybe? I can't— my head hurts too much to think. I don't know, leave me alone, I feel sick...

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Yes, start him on oxygen by nasal cannula — his sats are down to 91 on room air after the head injury.
